questions.question: In the formula I = P × r × t, the principal P is $500, the interest rate is 4% per year (written as the decimal 0.04), and the time t is 2 years. How much simple interest is earned?
questions.explain: Multiply all three parts once: 500 × 0.04 × 2 = 40. The usual trap is using 4 instead of 0.04, which makes the answer 100 times too big; the $540 answer is the whole balance, not the interest.

questions.question: In I = P × r × t, the principal is $600, the rate is 5% per year, and the time is 6 months. Write 6 months as a fraction of a year, then find the simple interest.
questions.explain: 6 months is 6/12 = 0.5 of a year, and 5% is 0.05, so I = 600 × 0.05 × 0.5 = 15. The big trap is putting t = 6 into the formula, which counts 6 whole years instead of half a year.

questions.question: A loan of $800 charges 12% simple interest per year and is paid back after 18 months. Which calculation gives the simple interest?
questions.explain: Turn the percent into a decimal (12% = 0.12) and the months into years (18/12 = 1.5), so the calculation is 800 × 0.12 × 1.5. Leaving 18 in as the time treats it as 18 years.

questions.question: In I = P × r × t, the principal is $400, the rate is 6% per year, and the time is 9 months. How much simple interest is earned?
questions.explain: 9 months is 9/12 = 0.75 of a year, so I = 400 × 0.06 × 0.75 = 18. Careful: 9 months is not 0.9 of a year, and it is not 9 years.

questions.question: Chloe deposits $1250 from her summer job into a savings account that pays 2.4% simple interest per year. She leaves the money there for 8 months. How much interest does she earn?
questions.explain: Use t = 8/12 = 2/3 of a year and r = 0.024: I = 1250 × 0.024 × 2/3 = 20. Using t = 8 (months as years) or r = 2.4 both blow the answer up far past what a small account could earn.

questions.question: Marco puts $900 into a savings account paying 3.5% simple interest per year and leaves it for 2 years. What is the total amount in the account at the end?
questions.explain: First the interest: 900 × 0.035 × 2 = 63, then add it to the principal for a balance of 963. The $63 answer stops at the interest and forgets to add the original deposit back on.

questions.question: Nadia deposits $2400 in a savings account that pays 1.5% simple interest per year. After 18 months she withdraws just the interest to pay for a bus pass. How much interest does she withdraw?
questions.explain: 18 months is 18/12 = 1.5 years and 1.5% is 0.015, so I = 2400 × 0.015 × 1.5 = 54. Watch the two different 1.5s: one is the rate as a decimal, the other is the time in years.

questions.question: Owen deposits $2000 in a savings account paying 4.5% simple interest per year. After 4 months he takes everything out to buy a bike. How much money does he take out?
questions.explain: 4 months is 4/12 = 1/3 of a year, so I = 2000 × 0.045 × 1/3 = 30, and he withdraws 2000 + 30 = 2030. The interest alone is only $30, so a balance in the thousands must include the principal.

questions.question: Kaito finds the simple interest on $1200 at 3% per year for 9 months. He writes I = 1200 × 0.03 × 9 = $324. What is wrong with his work?
options: He used 9 as the time; 9 months is 9/12 = 0.75 year, so I = $27.
Nothing is wrong; the money sat for 9 months, so the time must be 9.
He should have used 3, not 0.03, since the rate is 3 percent a year.
He should have added $1200 to the interest, since I means new total.
questions.explain: Time in I = Prt must be in years, so 9 months becomes 0.75 and I = 1200 × 0.03 × 0.75 = 27. His decimal rate of 0.03 was right; only the time was left in months.

questions.question: Maya deposits a $1800 birthday gift into a savings account paying 2.5% simple interest per year and leaves it untouched for 10 months. She then wants to buy a $1830 laptop. Can she pay for it from that account?
options: Yes - she will have $2250.00, which is enough.
Yes - she will have $1837.50, which is enough.
No - she will have only $37.50, not enough.
Yes - she will have $5550.00, which is enough.
questions.explain: Interest is 1800 × 0.025 × 10/12 = 37.50, and the account holds 1800 + 37.50 = 1837.50, which covers the $1830 laptop with $7.50 left. The $37.50 is only the interest earned, not everything in the account.

questions.question: Jordan has $2000 to save. Account A pays 3% simple interest per year and he would leave the money 8 months. Account B pays 2% simple interest per year and he would leave the money 15 months. Which account earns more interest, and by how much?
questions.explain: Account A gives 2000 × 0.03 × 8/12 = 40 and Account B gives 2000 × 0.02 × 15/12 = 50, so B wins by $10. A higher rate does not automatically win, because the longer time makes up the difference.

questions.question: Ava puts $850 in a savings account paying 4% simple interest per year. After 6 months she says, my account has $17 in it. What is the error?
options: The interest is $204, because the time in the formula is 6.
The interest is $1700, because the rate in the formula is 4.
She is right; $17 is the whole balance after the 6 months.
$17 is the interest earned; the account holds $867 in all.
questions.explain: With t = 0.5 year, I = 850 × 0.04 × 0.5 = 17, but that is the interest only, so the balance is 850 + 17 = 867. Always check whether the question wants the interest or the new total.
